learning_activity_name: Describe the concept of the cell (cell theory, organelles and biological molecules)
sla_name: The cell: theory, organelles and biological molecules
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of the cell is correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Stains|Scalpel/ razor blade/ knife|Stirrer|Beakers|Heat source|Droppers|Thermometer|Measuring cylinder|Microscope|Its accessories|Water bath
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function of all living organisms, and it contains organelles and molecules that carry out life processes.
sla_notes_details: Cell theory states that all organisms are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life and that new cells arise from existing cells. Eukaryotic cells contain a nucleus, mitochondria (aerobic respiration, cristae and matrix), rough endoplasmic reticulum (protein synthesis), smooth ER (lipid synthesis), Golgi apparatus (modification and packaging), lysosomes (digestion), ribosomes, and in plants chloroplasts, a cellulose cell wall and a large vacuole; prokaryotic cells have a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes and no membrane-bound organelles. The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that control transport. Biological molecules include carbohydrates (monosaccharides, disaccharides, starch, glycogen, cellulose), lipids (triglycerides and phospholipids), proteins (amino acids joined by peptide bonds, with primary to quaternary structure), enzymes as protein catalysts that lower activation energy, and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). Cell size is measured using magnification = image size / actual size with the light and electron microscope.
sla_notes_illustrations: An animal cell in a drawing is 30 mm long and the actual cell is 15 µm, so the magnification is 30 000 / 15 = x2000. Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch, Benedict's solution gives an orange-red precipitate with reducing sugars and biuret reagent turns violet with proteins.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding cells helps to explain digestion of food, how vaccines and antibiotics work, and why unhealthy diets that are high in fats and sugars affect the body.
sla_exercise: State two points of cell theory.::All living things are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; new cells come only from pre-existing cells.||Name the organelle where aerobic respiration takes place and give the reason it is called the powerhouse.::Mitochondrion; it produces most of the cell's ATP.||Which reagent is used to test for a reducing sugar and what positive result is seen?::Benedict's reagent, which gives a brick-red or orange precipitate on heating.

learning_activity_name: Explain the physiology of photosynthesis (mechanism of light reaction and dark reaction in C3 and C4 plants)
sla_name: Physiology of photosynthesis
sla_assessment_criteria: Physiology of photosynthesis is clearly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Potted plants|Charts|Diagrams|Illustrations showing physiology of photosynthesis
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants convert light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrates.
sla_notes_details: The overall equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ in the presence of light and chlorophyll. In the light-dependent reaction in the thylakoid membranes, chlorophyll absorbs light (mainly red and blue), water is split by photolysis (2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂), electrons pass along the electron transport chain producing ATP by photophosphorylation, and NADP is reduced to NADPH; cyclic photophosphorylation makes only ATP. In the light-independent reaction (Calvin cycle) in the stroma, CO₂ is fixed by RuBP with the enzyme rubisco to give two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (GP), which are reduced using ATP and NADPH to triose phosphate, and RuBP is regenerated; some triose phosphate forms glucose. C4 plants (maize, sugarcane) first fix CO₂ into oxaloacetate in mesophyll cells using PEP carboxylase and transfer it to bundle sheath cells, which reduces photorespiration and makes them efficient in hot, bright conditions. Limiting factors are light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature.
sla_notes_illustrations: In an experiment with pondweed, counting bubbles per minute shows that the rate of photosynthesis increases as the lamp is brought closer, then levels off when another factor such as CO₂ becomes limiting. Maize, a C4 plant, has a higher rate at 35 °C than beans, a C3 plant.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers increase yields by giving crops adequate light, water and spacing and by growing efficient crops such as maize and sugarcane in hot regions, and greenhouses raise CO₂ levels.
sla_exercise: Where do the light-dependent reactions take place?::In the thylakoid membranes (grana) of the chloroplast.||Name the enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle and the first product.::Rubisco fixes CO₂ with RuBP to give glycerate 3-phosphate (GP).||Give one advantage of the C4 pathway.::It concentrates CO₂ around rubisco and reduces photorespiration, so it is efficient in hot, bright conditions.

sla_name: Epithelial tissues and their digestive role
sla_assessment_criteria: Structure of epithelia tissue in relation to its digestive role are clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Microscope|Microscope slides|Diagrams|Charts showing structure of epithelia tissue in relation to its digestive role
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Epithelial tissues cover body surfaces and line organs, and those of the alimentary canal are adapted to protect, secrete and absorb.
sla_notes_details: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin single layer for diffusion. Simple columnar epithelium lines the stomach and intestine and has cells joined by tight junctions. In the ileum the surface has villi and cells with microvilli (the brush border), giving a very large surface area for absorption; the cells contain many mitochondria to provide ATP for active transport, and lacteals and capillaries below carry away absorbed nutrients. Goblet cells scattered among the columnar cells secrete mucus for lubrication and protection against enzymes and acid. In the stomach, gastric glands secrete HCl, pepsinogen and mucus, and the epithelium is protected by a mucus layer and rapid replacement of cells every few days. The oesophagus has stratified squamous epithelium to withstand abrasion. Disorders include peptic ulcers due to Helicobacter pylori, gastritis, diarrhoea and malabsorption.
sla_notes_illustrations: Villi in the small intestine increase the absorbing surface to about 250 m², roughly the area of a tennis court. If mucus is damaged, pepsin and hydrochloric acid digest the stomach wall, causing an ulcer.
sla_notes_daily_life: Eating balanced meals, taking treatment for ulcers, avoiding excess alcohol and painkillers and maintaining clean water and hygiene protect the lining of the digestive tract.
sla_exercise: Name the epithelial cells that produce mucus in the intestine.::Goblet cells.||How is the ileum epithelium adapted for absorption?::Villi and microvilli give a large surface area, cells are thin with many mitochondria, and a rich supply of blood capillaries and lacteals carries nutrients away.||Suggest a cause of peptic ulcers.::Infection by Helicobacter pylori, or damage of the protective mucus layer by acid, alcohol or some drugs.

learning_activity_name: Describe the physiology of gaseous exchange and respiration in mammals (transportation of gases, aerobic and anaerobic respiration mechanisms)
sla_name: Gaseous exchange and respiration in mammals
sla_assessment_criteria: Physiology of gaseous exchange and respiration in mammals is correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts|Pictures|Diagrams|Models|Videos showing physiology of gaseous exchange|Respiration in mammals
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Mammals take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide through the lungs, and cells use oxygen to release energy from food by respiration.
sla_notes_details: Air moves through the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to alveoli, which are lined with thin squamous epithelium surrounded by capillaries, giving a short diffusion distance and a large surface area; ventilation is by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. Oxygen is transported as oxyhaemoglobin (HbO₂); the oxygen dissociation curve is S-shaped and shifts right with high CO₂ and low pH (Bohr effect), releasing more oxygen to active tissues. Foetal haemoglobin and myoglobin have higher affinity. Carbon dioxide is carried mainly as hydrogencarbonate ions formed in red cells by carbonic anhydrase, with the chloride shift maintaining balance, and some as carbaminohaemoglobin. Aerobic respiration has glycolysis (cytoplasm), link reaction, Krebs cycle (matrix) and oxidative phosphorylation (cristae), giving up to 30-32 ATP per glucose. Anaerobic respiration gives lactate in mammals (2 ATP) and ethanol and CO₂ in yeast; oxygen debt is repaid after exercise. Respiratory quotient is CO₂ produced / O₂ used, 1.0 for carbohydrate and about 0.7 for fats.
sla_notes_illustrations: During exercise, muscles produce lactic acid, breathing rate rises to repay the oxygen debt and the lactate is converted back to glucose in the liver. The RQ of a runner burning glucose is 1.0 whereas a resting person burning mixed food has an RQ of about 0.85.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowledge of respiration explains why athletes train for endurance, why smoking damages alveoli, why high altitudes cause breathlessness and how yeast is used in brewing and baking.
sla_exercise: State the net ATP yield from aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule.::About 30-32 ATP (older texts 38).||What is the Bohr effect?::A rise in CO₂ concentration lowers blood pH and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen to tissues.||Name the end product of anaerobic respiration in muscles.::Lactic acid (lactate).

sla_name: Gaseous exchange in plants and stomatal mechanism
sla_assessment_criteria: Concept of gaseous exchange in plants is clearly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Commelina sp|Hand lens|Microscope|Microscope slides|Slide cover|Knife/ razor blade|Charts|Diagrams|Videos on plant adaptations
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Plants exchange gases through stomata, and opening and closing of these pores controls water loss and carbon dioxide intake.
sla_notes_details: Each stoma is bounded by two guard cells with thick inner walls and radially arranged cellulose microfibrils. In light, potassium ions are actively taken into guard cells (with H⁺ pumped out and chloride and malate accumulating), lowering the water potential, so water enters by osmosis, guard cells become turgid, bow apart and the stoma opens. In darkness or in water stress, abscisic acid causes K⁺ efflux, guard cells lose turgor and the stoma closes. Theories include the starch-sugar theory (starch converted to sugar in light), the potassium ion theory (active K⁺ uptake) and the role of CO₂ concentration in the guard cells. Stomata are more numerous on the lower epidermis of dicot leaves, and in xerophytes are sunken or few. Lenticels in stems and pneumatophores in mangroves also allow gaseous exchange. Transpiration rate is measured using a potometer and is affected by light, temperature, humidity and wind.
sla_notes_illustrations: When the epidermis of Commelina leaves is placed in a hypertonic sucrose solution, the guard cells lose water and the stomata close; in distilled water they open. A leaf loses more water on a hot, dry and windy day than on a cool, humid day.
sla_notes_daily_life: Gardeners water plants in the evening or use mulch to reduce water loss through stomata, and farmers select drought-resistant crops with fewer stomata or thick cuticles.
sla_exercise: Explain how stomata open in the light.::Guard cells actively take up K⁺, which lowers the water potential; water enters by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid and bend apart, opening the pore.||Name the hormone that causes stomata to close during water stress.::Abscisic acid.||Why do most stomata occur on the lower surface of dicot leaves?::Less water is lost as the lower surface is cooler and not directly exposed to sunlight.

learning_activity_name: Describe the physiology of coordination (mechanism of transmission of nerve impulse, seeing, hearing and body balance)
sla_name: Physiology of coordination
sla_assessment_criteria: Physiology of coordination is clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts|Pictures|Diagrams|Models showing physiology of coordination
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Coordination is the working together of the nervous and endocrine systems to respond to changes inside and outside the body.
sla_notes_details: A nerve impulse is an action potential: the resting membrane potential is about -70 mV, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump; stimulation opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels causing depolarisation to about +40 mV, followed by repolarisation by K⁺ efflux and a refractory period; impulses obey the all-or-none law and travel faster in myelinated axons by saltatory conduction. At a synapse, the impulse triggers calcium entry and release of a neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine, which diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the next neuron. The eye focuses light by the cornea and lens onto the retina, where rods (dim light, rhodopsin) and cones (colour vision) convert light into impulses that pass along the optic nerve; accommodation involves ciliary muscles. The ear detects sound with the eardrum, ossicles and cochlea whose hair cells produce impulses, and the semicircular canals and utricle detect head movement and body balance.
sla_notes_illustrations: When the light is bright, the pupil constricts by reflex: the retina sends impulses along the optic nerve to the brain, motor impulses go to the circular iris muscles and the pupil becomes smaller. A person who spins and stops feels dizzy because fluid in the semicircular canals continues to move.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reflexes protect us from danger, hearing and vision aids help people with disabilities, and knowledge of neurotransmitters helps in understanding the effects of drugs and poisons such as organophosphate pesticides.
sla_exercise: What is the resting potential of a neuron?::About -70 mV, with the inside negative relative to the outside.||Why is impulse conduction faster in myelinated neurons?::The impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), so depolarisation occurs only at the nodes.||Which part of the inner ear detects body balance?::The semicircular canals (with the utricle and saccule).

sla_name: Synthetic phytohormones: application and role
sla_assessment_criteria: Application or role of synthetic phytohormones are clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Manila paper|Marker pens
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Synthetic plant growth regulators imitate natural hormones and are widely used to increase agricultural productivity.
sla_notes_details: Natural phytohormones include auxins (cell elongation, apical dominance), gibberellins (stem elongation, seed germination), cytokinins (cell division, delay of leaf senescence), abscisic acid (dormancy, stomatal closure) and ethene (fruit ripening). Synthetic auxins such as IAA analogues NAA and IBA are used in rooting powders for cuttings; 2,4-D is a selective herbicide killing broad-leaved weeds in cereal fields by causing uncontrolled growth. Gibberellic acid is used to produce seedless grapes and to speed up malting of barley. Cytokinins prolong the life of cut flowers and vegetables. Ethephon releases ethene to ripen bananas, tomatoes and pineapples evenly, and synthetic auxins prevent premature fruit fall. Risks include residues in food, damage to non-target plants and environmental pollution, so recommended doses and safe handling are important.
sla_notes_illustrations: A gardener dips cuttings of hibiscus in rooting powder containing IBA and roots appear within two weeks, while cuttings without it take much longer or fail. Green bananas sprayed with ethephon in a closed room ripen uniformly in three days.
sla_notes_daily_life: Nurseries, flower farms, horticulture exports and weed control on maize and rice farms use synthetic plant hormones.
sla_exercise: Name one synthetic auxin used as a weed killer.::2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid).||What is the role of ethephon in fruit production?::It releases ethene which speeds up and evens out fruit ripening.||State one danger of misusing synthetic hormones.::Residues in food, harm to non-target plants and pollution of soil and water.

learning_activity_name: Explain the concept of regulation in mammals (feedback mechanisms, urine formation and osmoregulation)
sla_name: Regulation in mammals: feedback, urine formation and osmoregulation
sla_assessment_criteria: Concept of regulation in mammals is correctly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Models|Diagrams|Charts showing the mechanisms of regulation in mammals
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment of the body relatively constant, using feedback mechanisms and the kidneys.
sla_notes_details: Negative feedback restores a factor to its set point; examples are the control of body temperature by the hypothalamus (vasodilation and sweating when hot, vasoconstriction and shivering when cold) and blood glucose by insulin and glucagon. Positive feedback amplifies a change, for example uterine contractions during birth by oxytocin. The nephron forms urine by ultrafiltration at the glomerulus (pressure forces water, glucose, urea and salts into the Bowman's capsule but not proteins), selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule (all glucose, amino acids and most water and salts), the loop of Henle that creates a concentration gradient by a countercurrent multiplier, and the distal tubule and collecting duct where water reabsorption is controlled. When blood water potential falls, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus cause the pituitary to release ADH, making the collecting duct more permeable to water and producing small amounts of concentrated urine; the reverse occurs when there is excess water. Aldosterone regulates sodium. Kidney failure is treated by dialysis or transplant.
sla_notes_illustrations: After a hot day without drinking, ADH increases and the urine is dark and concentrated; after drinking a large amount of water ADH falls and dilute urine is passed. In diabetes, glucose exceeds the reabsorption capacity and appears in urine.
sla_notes_daily_life: Drinking enough water, knowing the effects of alcohol (which inhibits ADH and causes dehydration) and understanding dialysis and diabetes management use knowledge of regulation.
sla_exercise: Name the hormone that increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct.::Anti-diuretic hormone (ADH).||Where does ultrafiltration take place in the nephron?::Between the glomerulus capillaries and the Bowman's capsule.||Explain negative feedback using body temperature.::When body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation cool the body; when it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction warm it, returning it to the set point.

sla_teaching_aids: Specimens of living organisms (preserved or fresh)|Simple constructed keys|Prepared identification keys of plants|Animals|Pictures|Photographs showing principles of binomial nomenclature

sla_notes_intro: Classification arranges organisms into groups based on similarities to make their study orderly and to show evolutionary relationships.
sla_notes_details: Artificial systems group organisms by a few visible features, natural systems use many features, and phylogenetic systems reflect evolutionary relationships using fossils, comparative anatomy, cytology and molecular data such as DNA and protein sequences. The taxonomic hierarchy from the largest group is domain, kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus and species. A species is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Three domains are recognised: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, and the five-kingdom system of Whittaker separates Monera, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Taxonomy uses dichotomous keys, in which paired statements lead to identification, and modern techniques of DNA barcoding.
sla_notes_illustrations: The lion is classified as Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae, Genus Panthera, species leo. A horse and a donkey mate to produce a sterile mule, so they are separate species.
sla_notes_daily_life: Botanists, doctors and farmers use classification to identify pests, medicinal plants, disease-causing microbes and to conserve endangered species.
sla_exercise: Arrange the taxonomic ranks from kingdom to species.::Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.||Define a species.::A group of organisms that interbreed naturally and produce fertile offspring.||What is a dichotomous key?::An identification tool with paired contrasting statements that lead the user step by step to the name of an organism.

sla_notes_intro: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a universal two-part scientific name, introduced by Carolus Linnaeus.
sla_notes_details: The scientific name consists of the genus name, with a capital first letter, followed by the species name in lower case, and both are written in italics or underlined when handwritten, for example Homo sapiens. Names are in Latin or latinised, must be unique for each species and are regulated by the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature and the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants. The genus is a noun and the species epithet is often an adjective describing a feature, origin or the discoverer. The name may be followed by the author's name, and when written a second time the genus is abbreviated to its initial letter (H. sapiens). Subspecies and varieties add a third name. The hierarchy of taxa allows placing each species in its genus, family and higher groups.
sla_notes_illustrations: Zea mays is maize, Mangifera indica is mango, Panthera leo is lion and Anopheles gambiae is the malaria mosquito. Local names differ: mahindi in Swahili and corn in America, but Zea mays is understood everywhere.
sla_notes_daily_life: Scientists, herbalists and traders use scientific names to avoid confusion when many common names exist for the same organism in different languages.
sla_exercise: Write the correct scientific name format for the human being.::Homo sapiens (genus with a capital letter, species with lower case, both italicised or underlined).||Why are scientific names in Latin?::Latin is an international, unchanging language which makes names universal and stable.||Who developed the binomial system of naming?::Carolus Linnaeus.

sla_notes_intro: Correct scientific names are used in many fields to identify organisms accurately and communicate safely.
sla_notes_details: In forestry, timber species such as Tectona grandis (teak), Pinus patula and Acacia polyacantha are named to control trade, forest inventories and conservation of endangered trees like Dalbergia melanoxylon (African blackwood). In medicine, disease-causing organisms are identified by their names, for example Plasmodium falciparum for malaria, Vibrio cholerae for cholera and Mycobacterium tuberculosis for tuberculosis, and herbal medicines are identified by species such as Artemisia annua and Moringa oleifera. In agriculture, crop varieties, pests and beneficial organisms are named accurately, for example Coffea arabica, Zea mays, Oryza sativa, the pest Busseola fusca (maize stalk borer) and the pollinator Apis mellifera. Precise names are needed for quarantine, seed certification, patents, research and biodiversity records.
sla_notes_illustrations: Customs officers check that an export of Coffea arabica is not confused with other Coffea species, and a laboratory report that names Plasmodium falciparum guides the choice of antimalarial drug.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers reading pesticide labels, herbalists recommending plants and forest officers checking timber licences use scientific names.
sla_exercise: Give the scientific name of the malaria parasite that causes the most severe malaria.::Plasmodium falciparum.||Why do forest officers use scientific names for timber species?::To identify species accurately for licences, trade and conservation because common names vary between places.||Write the scientific name of maize.::Zea mays.

sla_notes_intro: The five kingdoms are distinguished by cell type, body organisation, nutrition and reproduction.
sla_notes_details: Monera (bacteria and cyanobacteria) are prokaryotic, unicellular and have a peptidoglycan cell wall. Protoctista are eukaryotic, mostly unicellular or simple multicellular, and include protozoa (Amoeba, Plasmodium), algae (Spirogyra) and slime moulds. Fungi are eukaryotic, heterotrophic by absorption, have chitin cell walls and hyphae forming a mycelium, and reproduce by spores (Rhizopus, yeast, mushrooms). Plantae are multicellular autotrophs with cellulose walls, divided into Bryophyta (mosses, no vascular tissue), Filicinophyta (ferns), Coniferophyta (cone-bearing) and Angiospermophyta (flowering plants, monocots and dicots). Animalia are multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls and include Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda (insects, arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods) and Chordata, whose classes are Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. Characteristics used include symmetry, body cavity, segmentation, skeleton and type of reproduction.
sla_notes_illustrations: A tapeworm belongs to Platyhelminthes because it is a flatworm with a flattened, unsegmented body, while an earthworm is a segmented annelid; a housefly, with three pairs of legs and a body in three parts, is an insect, and a bat is a mammal because it has hair and mammary glands.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising groups helps to control pests and diseases (mosquitoes, worms), to use useful fungi such as yeast and mushrooms and to conserve wildlife.
sla_exercise: Give two features of fungi.::They have chitin cell walls and feed heterotrophically by absorption through hyphae; they reproduce by spores.||Name the classes of the phylum Chordata.::Pisces (fish), Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia.||State two features of arthropods.::Jointed legs and an exoskeleton of chitin; segmented body.

sla_notes_intro: Biological investigations require observation, measurement, recording of data and clear reporting.
sla_notes_details: Observation involves using the senses, hand lens and microscope, and making labelled drawings with the title, magnification and scale. Measurement includes length, mass, volume, time, temperature and pH using appropriate instruments and units, with repeats to improve reliability. Sampling methods such as quadrats, transects and mark-release-recapture are used in the field. Data are collected in tables with headings and units, processed by mean, percentage and rate, and presented by graphs (line, bar, histogram, scatter) with labelled axes. Interpretation notes trends, and conclusions are related to the hypothesis. A report includes the title, aim, hypothesis, materials, procedure, results, discussion, conclusion and references, written in the past tense and passive voice. Safety and ethics, such as the humane treatment of animals and disposal of biological waste, are observed.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a study of the effect of temperature on catalase activity in liver or potato, students measure the height of froth after 2 minutes at 10, 20, 30, 40 and 60 °C, record readings three times, calculate the means and plot a graph showing an optimum near 37 °C for animal liver.
sla_notes_daily_life: Nurses, farmers, veterinarians and environmental officers record and interpret observations and measurements in their daily work.
sla_exercise: State two things that should be included in a biological drawing.::A title and labels (also magnification or scale, and clear continuous lines).||Why should measurements be repeated?::To detect errors and calculate an average, improving reliability.||Which sampling tool is used to estimate the population of plants in a grassland?::A quadrat.

sla_notes_intro: In an independent investigation students choose a question, plan a method, carry it out and evaluate the results.
sla_notes_details: The steps are: choose a testable question, form a hypothesis, identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables, select apparatus and organisms, write a step-by-step method with a control experiment, plan safety and the number of replicates, collect data, analyse, draw conclusions and evaluate limitations such as sample size and uncontrolled variables. Suitable investigations are the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis, the effect of pH on the activity of amylase, the rate of transpiration under different conditions, the germination of seeds at different temperatures or the vitamin C content of fruits. A statistical test such as a t-test or chi-squared test may be used to judge whether differences are significant. The work is documented in a logbook.
sla_notes_illustrations: To test the effect of light on transpiration, a potometer is set up with a leafy shoot, the distance moved by the air bubble in 5 minutes is measured near a lamp at 10, 20 and 30 cm and in the shade, and results are graphed, showing that transpiration increases with light intensity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Agricultural extension officers testing fertilizers, brewers testing yeast conditions and health workers checking water quality follow similar investigation procedures.
sla_exercise: Identify the independent variable in an experiment on the effect of temperature on the rate of enzyme reaction.::Temperature.||Why is a control experiment included?::To show that the observed effect is due to the variable being tested and not to other factors.||Suggest one limitation of a small sample size.::The results may not be representative or reliable, so conclusions are weak.

sla_notes_intro: Dissections, microscope studies and physiological experiments give direct evidence of how organs and systems work.

Physiological investigations include food tests, enzyme activity of amylase and catalase, the effect of light intensity, CO₂ and temperature on photosynthesis using pondweed, testing leaves for starch after de-starching, the products of respiration using lime water or hydrogencarbonate indicator, the rate of gaseous exchange using a respirometer, and osmosis using potato cylinders. Observations are recorded with drawings and results are interpreted. Ethical procedures require the use of humane animal handling and safe disposal of specimens and chemicals.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a respirometer with germinating seeds and soda lime, the level of coloured liquid rises as oxygen is absorbed and CO₂ is removed; the distance moved per minute measures the rate of oxygen uptake, which is higher at 30 °C than at 10 °C.
sla_notes_daily_life: Skills used here are useful for future doctors, nurses, laboratory technologists and veterinary officers.

sla_name: Transport of materials in plants
sla_assessment_criteria: Physiology and theories underlying transportation of materials in plants are clearly explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Microscopes slides|Microscope|Charts|Diagrams showing vascular tissues|Transparent plastic tube|Seedlings|Simulations|Leaf such as Commelina sp|Slide cover|Charts showing opening|Closing of stomata
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Plants transport water and minerals upwards in the xylem and organic solutes in the phloem, driven by physical and metabolic forces.
sla_notes_details: Water enters root hairs by osmosis down a water potential gradient and crosses the cortex by the apoplast, symplast and vacuolar pathways until the Casparian strip forces it through the endodermis cells into the xylem. Movement up the xylem is explained by the cohesion-tension theory: transpiration from the leaves lowers the water potential, creating a tension that pulls a continuous column of water held together by cohesion of water molecules and adhesion to lignified walls; root pressure gives a small additional push. Xylem vessels are dead, lignified and hollow. Minerals enter by diffusion and active transport. Translocation of sucrose in phloem sieve tubes is explained by the mass flow hypothesis: sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source (leaves) with the help of companion cells, lowering the water potential and drawing in water, producing high hydrostatic pressure that pushes sap to the sink (roots, fruits) where sucrose is unloaded. Evidence includes ringing experiments, aphid stylets and radioactive tracers such as ¹⁴CO₂. Transpiration is measured with a potometer and is affected by light, humidity, temperature and wind.
sla_notes_illustrations: When a bark ring is removed from a woody stem, the bark swells above the cut because sugars from the leaves accumulate there, showing that phloem transports organic solutes downwards. A cut stem placed in eosin dye shows the dye moving up the xylem within minutes.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers irrigate crops during dry spells, florists put cut flowers in water, and foresters know that ring-barking kills trees, all based on transport in plants.
sla_exercise: Name the tissue that transports water in plants.::Xylem.||State the role of the Casparian strip.::It is a waterproof suberin band in the endodermis walls that forces water and minerals to pass through the selectively permeable cell membranes.||Explain the mass flow hypothesis in one sentence.::Sucrose is loaded into phloem at the source, causing water to enter and create pressure that pushes the sap towards the sink where sucrose is unloaded.

sla_name: Blood circulation in vertebrates
sla_assessment_criteria: Mechanisms of blood circulation in vertebrates are correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts|Picture|Diagram of cardiac muscle|Microscope slides|Microscope|Simulations|Models showing circulatory systems
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Circulatory systems carry oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes, and they vary in complexity among vertebrates.
sla_notes_details: Fish have a single circulation: blood passes once through the heart (one atrium and one ventricle) to the gills and then to the body, so pressure is reduced after the gills. Amphibians and most reptiles have a double circulation with three-chambered hearts and some mixing, while birds and mammals have four chambers that completely separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, so the pulmonary and systemic circuits work at different pressures. The cardiac cycle has atrial systole, ventricular systole and diastole, with valves preventing backflow; the heart beat is myogenic, started by the sino-atrial node and coordinated by the atrioventricular node and Purkinje fibres, and its rate is controlled by the medulla oblongata through the sympathetic and vagus nerves. In the foetus, blood bypasses the lungs through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, and the placenta exchanges materials with maternal blood by diffusion without the two bloods mixing; foetal haemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity. Tissue fluid forms at the arterial end of capillaries by hydrostatic pressure and returns partly by osmosis and through lymph vessels.
sla_notes_illustrations: A mammalian heart beats about 70 times per minute and pumps 70 cm³ each beat, so the cardiac output is 70 x 70 = 4900 cm³ per minute (about 4.9 dm³). Exercise raises heart rate to over 150 beats per minute and the output increases several times.
sla_notes_daily_life: Checking pulse rate, knowing the effect of exercise, understanding hypertension, heart disease and blood pressure, and caring for pregnancy are practical uses of circulation knowledge.
sla_exercise: How many chambers has the heart of a mammal?::Four: two atria and two ventricles.||Explain why a double circulation is more efficient than a single circulation.::Blood returns to the heart after gaseous exchange and is pumped again at high pressure to the body, so tissues receive oxygenated blood faster.||Name the structure that sets the pace of the heart beat.::The sino-atrial node (pacemaker).

sla_teaching_aids: Charts|Diagram|Simulations|Models|Microscope slides|Charts/ Diagrams showing various patterns of growth in plants|Microscope
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Growth in plants is an irreversible increase in size and dry mass, resulting from cell division, elongation and differentiation.
sla_notes_details: The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) and mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) followed by cytokinesis. Growth occurs at meristems: apical meristems give primary growth in length, and lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium) give secondary growth in thickness, forming secondary xylem (wood) and secondary phloem, with annual rings showing seasonal growth. Growth is measured by increase in length, fresh mass or dry mass, and the pattern is sigmoid (lag, log and stationary phases) for the whole plant. Seed dormancy is caused by hard coats, inhibitors such as abscisic acid or immature embryos, and is broken by scarification, stratification, light and gibberellins; seed viability is tested with tetrazolium chloride, which turns living embryos red, and germination tests. Germination may be epigeal (cotyledons above ground, as in beans) or hypogeal (cotyledons remain below, as in maize). Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and light affect the pattern of growth and phototropism.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a germination experiment with 50 bean seeds, 45 seeds germinate so the viability is 90%. Bean seedlings placed near a window bend toward the light because auxin accumulates on the shaded side, causing greater elongation there.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers test seed viability before planting, soak or scratch seeds to hasten germination, and prune trees to control growth, and timber is obtained from secondary growth.
sla_exercise: Name the two lateral meristems in a woody stem.::Vascular cambium and cork cambium.||How is seed dormancy broken by scarification?::Rubbing or nicking the hard seed coat allows water and oxygen to enter, so the embryo can germinate.||Which stain is used to test seed viability?::Tetrazolium chloride; living seeds turn red.

sla_teaching_aids: Microscope|Microscope slide|Charts|Diagrams|Models|Simulations|Showing various patterns of growth in animals
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Animals grow in different patterns, and many insects and amphibians change form through metamorphosis.
sla_notes_details: Growth curves may be sigmoid for many vertebrates, including humans, which show rapid growth in infancy and at puberty, or stepwise for arthropods, which grow only after moulting (ecdysis) because of the rigid exoskeleton. Growth may be isometric (all parts at the same rate) or allometric (parts at different rates, as in human head and limbs). Growth is measured by length, fresh mass or dry mass, the last being the most accurate but destroying the organism. Metamorphosis is a change from larva to adult: complete metamorphosis (holometabolous) has egg, larva, pupa and adult (butterflies, mosquitoes, flies), and incomplete metamorphosis (hemimetabolous) has egg, nymph and adult (locusts, cockroaches, dragonflies). Ecdysone triggers moulting, and juvenile hormone maintains larval features; in amphibians thyroxine controls the change from tadpole to frog. Human growth is controlled by growth hormone, thyroxine and sex hormones.
sla_notes_illustrations: A locust nymph moults five times, increasing its size after each moult before becoming an adult, while a caterpillar feeds greatly, pupates and emerges as a butterfly. A mosquito larva lives in water but the adult flies, which is why draining stagnant water controls malaria.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the life cycles of insects helps in controlling pests such as locusts, armyworm and mosquitoes, in rearing silkworms and honeybees, and in monitoring the growth of children.
sla_exercise: Give the stages of complete metamorphosis.::Egg, larva, pupa and adult.||Why do insects moult?::The exoskeleton cannot expand, so it is shed to allow the body to grow.||Which hormone controls metamorphosis in frogs?::Thyroxine.

sla_name: Reproduction in plants
sla_assessment_criteria: Mechanisms of reproduction in plants is correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Microscope slides|Microscope|Diagrams of endospermic|Nonendospermic seeds|Charts showing diagrams of life cycles of different plants

sla_notes_intro: Flowering plants reproduce sexually through flowers, seeds and fruits, and many also reproduce asexually.
sla_notes_details: Microsporogenesis in the anther gives pollen grains, each with a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus that divides to form two male gametes; megasporogenesis in the ovule gives an embryo sac with eight nuclei, including the egg cell, two polar nuclei and antipodal cells. Pollination (self or cross, by wind, insects, birds or water) transfers pollen to the stigma; the pollen tube grows down the style to the micropyle and double fertilisation follows: one male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote (2n) and the other with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit. Life cycles of selected plants show alternation of generations: in mosses the gametophyte (n) is dominant, in ferns the sporophyte is dominant with a small prothallus, and in angiosperms the gametophytes are reduced. Vegetative propagation by bulbs, tubers, rhizomes, cuttings and grafting produces clones.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a maize flower the pollen grain germinates on the silk (stigma), the pollen tube grows several centimetres, and each fertilised ovule becomes a grain, so each kernel on a cob needs one pollen grain. Cassava is propagated by stem cuttings, which produce plants identical to the parent.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers plan crop pollination by keeping bees, use cuttings and grafting to grow fruit trees, and understand seeds, fruits and food production.
sla_exercise: What is double fertilisation in flowering plants?::One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a zygote and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm nucleus.||Which generation is dominant in a fern?::The sporophyte.||Give two advantages of vegetative propagation.::Offspring are identical to the parent with desired traits, and it is faster than growing from seed.

sla_notes_intro: Animal reproduction involves gamete formation, fertilisation and development, controlled in mammals by hormones.
sla_notes_details: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules of the testis produces sperm by mitosis, growth, meiosis and differentiation, and is stimulated by FSH and testosterone. Oogenesis in the ovary produces an ovum through meiosis, which is completed only if fertilisation occurs. Fertilisation is external in fish and amphibians and internal in reptiles, birds and mammals; the acrosome reaction and cortical reaction ensure that only one sperm fuses with the egg. The menstrual cycle lasts about 28 days: FSH stimulates follicle growth and oestrogen secretion, a surge of LH causes ovulation about day 14, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone that maintains the uterus lining, and if no implantation occurs the hormones fall and menstruation follows. During pregnancy the placenta secretes hCG, oestrogen and progesterone, and oxytocin and prolactin control birth and lactation. The oestrus cycle in other mammals differs in that the female is receptive only at certain times and the endometrium is reabsorbed instead of shed. Contraceptive methods work by preventing ovulation, fertilisation or implantation.
sla_notes_illustrations: A woman with a regular 28-day cycle ovulates near day 14. Pregnancy tests detect hCG in urine, which is produced by the embryo soon after implantation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Family planning, understanding fertility problems, safe pregnancy and childcare and livestock breeding by artificial insemination all use knowledge of animal reproduction.
sla_exercise: Name the hormone whose surge triggers ovulation.::Luteinising hormone (LH).||What is the role of progesterone in the menstrual cycle and pregnancy?::It maintains the thickened uterine lining and prevents contractions so that implantation and pregnancy can continue.||Why is hCG measured in pregnancy tests?::It is secreted by the embryo after implantation and appears in urine only during pregnancy.

sla_notes_intro: Inheritance explains how genetic information in DNA is copied, expressed and passed from parents to offspring.
sla_notes_details: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands with base pairing A-T and G-C; genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins. DNA replication is semi-conservative: helicase unwinds the strands, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to each template strand in the 5' to 3' direction, and ligase joins fragments. Protein synthesis has transcription in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase makes mRNA from the template strand, and translation at ribosomes, where tRNA anticodons match mRNA codons and amino acids are joined by peptide bonds. Mendel's laws state segregation of alleles and independent assortment. In a dihybrid cross of two heterozygotes (AaBb x AaBb) the phenotype ratio is 9:3:3:1. Variations such as codominance (ABO blood groups), sex linkage (haemophilia and colour blindness), epistasis and linkage give modified ratios, and mutations (gene or chromosomal) may cause sickle cell anaemia or Down syndrome. The chi-squared test compares observed and expected ratios.
sla_notes_illustrations: In pea plants, round (R) is dominant to wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) to green (y). A cross RrYy x RrYy gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. If the template strand is TAC GGA, the mRNA is AUG CCU, coding for methionine then proline.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding inheritance helps in selecting crop varieties and livestock breeds, genetic counselling for conditions such as sickle cell disease, blood transfusion and paternity testing, and forensic DNA identification.
sla_exercise: State the base-pairing rule in DNA.::Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.||What is the expected phenotypic ratio in a dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes?::9:3:3:1.||Write the mRNA transcribed from the DNA template strand TAC.::AUG.

sla_assessment_criteria: Theories and mechanism underlying evolution are clearly explained.

sla_notes_intro: Evolution is the gradual change in the inherited characteristics of populations over generations, leading to the diversity of life.
sla_notes_details: Theories of the origin of life include special creation, spontaneous generation (disproved by Redi and Pasteur), the cosmozoic theory, and the chemical evolution theory of Oparin and Haldane, supported by the Miller-Urey experiment in which amino acids formed from simple gases and electric sparks. Organic evolution theories: Lamarck proposed use and disuse and inheritance of acquired characters, which is not supported by evidence; Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection, with overproduction, variation, struggle for existence, survival of the fittest and inheritance of favourable traits; the modern synthesis links this to genetics and mutations. Evidence for evolution comes from fossils (Archaeopteryx, horse series), comparative anatomy (homologous and analogous structures, vestigial organs), embryology, biochemistry (similarity of DNA and cytochrome c) and biogeography. Speciation happens when populations are isolated (allopatric) or become reproductively isolated in the same area (sympatric) and gene flow stops, and it may be aided by genetic drift and mutations. Examples of natural selection are industrial melanism in peppered moths, antibiotic resistance in bacteria and pesticide resistance in insects.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the peppered moth, dark forms became common in polluted areas of England because they were camouflaged on dark tree trunks and escaped predators, showing directional selection. In a hospital, repeated use of an antibiotic selects resistant bacteria which multiply.
sla_notes_daily_life: Evolution explains resistance to antibiotics and pesticides, informs breeding and conservation, and shows the relationship between humans and other species.
sla_exercise: State two points of Darwin's theory of natural selection.::There is variation among individuals and more offspring are produced than can survive, so those best adapted survive and pass on their traits.||Give one example of a homologous structure.::The forelimb of a human, bat, whale and horse, which share the same bone plan but differ in function.||What is allopatric speciation?::Formation of a new species after a population is separated by a geographical barrier so that gene flow stops.

sla_notes_intro: Ecology studies the relationships between organisms and their environment, and how ecosystems can be sustained.
sla_notes_details: Methods of studying ecosystems include quadrats for plants and slow-moving animals, line and belt transects along environmental gradients, pitfall traps and sweep nets for insects, and mark-release-recapture for mobile animals with population N = (M x n)/m, together with measurement of abiotic factors such as light, temperature, pH and moisture. Biodiversity is expressed as species richness and Simpson's index of diversity D = 1 - Σ(n/N)². Energy flows through food chains and food webs with only about 10% transferred between trophic levels, and nutrients cycle in the carbon and nitrogen cycles. Ecological succession is the gradual change in the community: primary succession begins on bare rock with pioneers such as lichens, then mosses, grasses, shrubs and finally the climax community; secondary succession occurs after disturbance such as fire. Conservation methods are in situ (national parks, game reserves, forest reserves, marine parks) and ex situ (botanic gardens, zoos, seed banks), with sustainable use, anti-poaching laws, community-based conservation and reforestation.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a mark-release-recapture study, 50 insects are marked; a second sample of 40 contains 10 marked, so the estimated population is 50 x 40/10 = 200. Serengeti and Ngorongoro are examples of conservation areas that protect biodiversity in Tanzania.
sla_notes_daily_life: Protecting forests and wildlife supports tourism, water catchment areas and climate regulation, and communities benefit from sustainable management of resources.
sla_exercise: Name the tool used to sample plants in a defined area.::A quadrat.||Define ecological succession.::The gradual and orderly change in the species composition of a community over time until a stable climax community is reached.||Give two examples of ex situ conservation.::Botanical gardens and seed banks (also zoos).

sla_name: Preparing and presenting a biological investigation report
sla_assessment_criteria: Biological investigations reports are clearly prepared following scientific procedure.
sla_teaching_aids: Note book|Pencil|Relevant text on scientific report writing procedure
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A report communicates the aim, method, findings and conclusions of a biological investigation so that others can judge and repeat the work.
sla_notes_details: The report contains the title, aim, hypothesis, materials, method with a labelled diagram, results with tables and graphs, analysis using calculations such as means, rates or percentages, discussion that explains results using biological principles, sources of error, conclusion, and references. Writing uses the past tense, the third person and precise scientific terms, with SI units and correct significant figures. Results are presented in graphs with axes labelled and units given and the type of graph chosen to fit the data. Oral presentations and posters may also be used to share the findings, with an introduction, main points and a conclusion, and answering questions from the audience. Honest reporting of the data and acknowledgement of sources are essential.
sla_notes_illustrations: After an experiment on enzyme activity, a report states: the rate of reaction increased from 0.5 cm³/min at 10 °C to 3.0 cm³/min at 37 °C and then dropped at 60 °C because the enzyme was denatured, which supports the hypothesis of an optimum temperature.
sla_notes_daily_life: Researchers, agricultural officers and laboratory technicians write reports for supervisors, donors and the public, and the same skills are needed in most careers.
sla_exercise: List the sections of a scientific report in order.::Title, aim, hypothesis, materials, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references.||Why is the past tense used in the method?::It describes work that has already been done.||Why should sources of error be discussed?::To show the limitations of the results and suggest how the investigation could be improved.

main_competence_name: Conduct biological investigations
specific_competence_name: Perform investigations on the anatomy and physiology of living organisms
learning_activity_name: Design and carry out anatomical and physiological investigations related to transportation in plants and animals, growth in plants and reproductive system
sla_name: Investigations on transport, growth and reproduction
sla_assessment_criteria: Anatomical and physiological investigations related to transportation in plants and animals, growth in plants and reproductive system are correctly designed and carried out.
sla_teaching_aids: Varieties of organisms|Microscope|Microscope slides|Laboratory reagents|Chemicals laboratory apparatti
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Investigations in Form Six focus on the physiology of transport and growth in plants and animals, and the structure of reproductive systems.
sla_notes_details: Practical work includes measuring the rate of transpiration with a potometer, tracing water in xylem with dyes, sectioning stems and roots to examine vascular tissues, ringing experiments to show phloem transport, studying the mammalian heart by dissection, and measuring pulse rate and blood pressure before and after exercise. Growth investigations involve measuring seedling length and dry mass over time, plotting growth curves, studying the effects of light and hormones on growth, and observing germination types. Reproductive investigations include examining flowers, dissecting to show the structure of stamens and carpels, observing pollen germination in sugar solution, studying fruits and seeds, and studying slides of the testis and ovary and models of the mammalian reproductive system. Data are recorded, graphed and discussed with an evaluation of errors.
sla_notes_illustrations: Pollen of Hibiscus is placed in 10% sucrose solution on a slide and after 30 minutes pollen tubes are seen through the microscope. The heart rate of a student rises from 72 to 120 beats per minute after two minutes of exercise and returns to normal after five minutes of rest.
sla_notes_daily_life: Health workers measure pulse and blood pressure, farmers test seed germination and horticulturists apply knowledge of pollination and propagation, all of which come from such investigations.
sla_exercise: Which instrument is used to measure the rate of water uptake of a shoot?::A potometer.||How can pollen germination be observed in the laboratory?::Place pollen grains in a sucrose solution (about 10%) on a slide and observe under the microscope after some time.||What happens to the heart rate during exercise and why?::It increases because muscles need more oxygen and glucose and must remove more CO₂ and heat.

main_competence_name: Conduct a project in Biology
specific_competence_name: Conduct a project in Biology
learning_activity_name: Complete and submit for assessment a scientific report of the project started in Form Five
sla_name: Completing and submitting the biology project report
sla_assessment_criteria: Scientific report of the project is clearly written and quality project product(s) are obtained.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples|Project guidelines|Sample of project reports|Biology based software
sla_references: TET(2023), BIOLOGY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The biology project designed in Form Five is completed with data analysis and a formal scientific report for assessment.
sla_notes_details: Students complete their field or laboratory work, verify the data, process it using statistics such as means, percentages, standard deviation and tests of significance, present results with graphs and interpret them in relation to the objectives and hypotheses. The report has a title page, declaration, acknowledgement, abstract, table of contents, introduction, literature review, methodology, results and analysis, discussion, conclusion, recommendations, references and appendices. Ethical rules such as safe handling of organisms, honesty and consent from communities are followed. The final work may be displayed at a school science exhibition or presented to teachers and the community for assessment.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group that studied the effect of botanical pesticides on aphids reports that a neem extract reduced aphid numbers by 70% compared with 5% in the control and recommends that farmers use the extract in a 10% solution for cheap pest control.
sla_notes_daily_life: Many food and health problems in communities can be solved when the findings of school projects are presented and applied by farmers and health workers.
sla_exercise: What is the purpose of the abstract of a report?::It gives a short summary of the aim, method, main results and conclusion.||Why should a project report include recommendations?::To advise how the findings can be applied or how further work can be improved.||Name one ethical principle to follow in a biology project.::Treat organisms humanely and dispose of waste safely; report data honestly.
